name: Sulphate Green
lede: Sulphate Green is a vivid bluish green from Ridgway's 1912 atlas; the books mention sulphates, which gave dyers and pigment makers several green and blue colors, but not this name.

sections.title: A chemical's name on a color
sections.body:
The record for the color is a list of atlases. Ridgway placed it on plate XIX, hue 39 prime, in 1912, and the ISCC-NBS system lists it at block 163 in 1955, where this swatch counts as "vivid bluish green", 3.2 CIEDE2000 units away [1]. Our sources do not say which sulphate the name refers to, and Ridgway's own scan is approximate [1].

Sulphate is a chemical word the dyer's trade knew well. Balfour-Paul's glossary defines copperas as hydrated ferrous sulphate, also called green vitriol, the iron salt used in the old "copperas" indigo vat [2]. The name may point to this family of salts, but that link is not documented [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Sulphate Green is rare in painting [3]. It appears in 13 of 23,781 paintings in our archive, 0.05 per cent, rarer than 79 per cent of the named colors, and the within-painting lens finds it in only 3 [3]. The earliest dated match is 1638 by Willem Ormea, 274 years before Ridgway's name, and the archive's early centuries are thin [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a look-alike hue and not proof of a pigment [3].

In printed English the words peak in the 1940s [4].

origin.named_after: origin undocumented; a sulphate salt is likely but unproven
